name: US Virgin Islands
summary: US Virgin Islands is a US territory, so a casket arriving from abroad is subject to the same federal CDC rules as the US mainland (42 CFR 71 expressly covers US Virgin Islands): the remains must be in a leak-proof container and, unless embalmed, travel with a death certificate stating the cause of death. A licensed local funeral home receives the remains after CBP clearance.
coffin: CDC requires all non-cremated remains to be fully contained in a leak-proof container (for example a casket with a leak-proof lining or a sealed metal transfer case). No territorial rule on zinc lining or witnessed sealing was found; the country of departure may impose a hermetically sealed zinc-lined coffin.
embalming: Not required by US federal rules for entry, but embalmed remains are exempt from the CDC death-certificate requirement. Remains of a person who died of certain infectious diseases may need a CDC import permit unless embalmed. Most departure countries and airlines require embalming anyway.
consular: No legalisation is required for entry. If a US citizen dies abroad, the US embassy or consulate can issue a Consular Report of Death Abroad and, where no death certificate exists, a Consular Mortuary Certificate. Foreign-language documents need an English translation.
arrival: CBP clears the remains at the first US port of entry, with CDC requirements checked against the documents. Under 42 CFR 71.55 the remains must go directly to a licensed mortuary, cemetery or crematory. The receiving funeral home then handles the local burial or cremation formalities with the Virgin Islands Department of Health Office of Vital Records and Statistics; the territory's own requirements are not published online.
private_aviation: Human remains on a private or charter flight need the same documents as airline cargo; the documents travel with the coffin and are presented to customs and health officials at the arrival airport. The coffin (typically about 2.2 m long, 70-100 kg once zinc-lined) must physically fit the aircraft's cargo door or a cabin configured for it, which rules out many light and midsize jets. An international arrival into US Virgin Islands must clear US Customs and Border Protection, so plan the flight to an airport where CBP clearance can be arranged in advance and have the receiving funeral home meet the aircraft. A flight from the US mainland is a domestic flight and needs no CBP entry, but the state burial-transit permit must travel with the remains.
export: Not published online. The Department of Health Office of Vital Records and Statistics registers deaths and works with funeral homes; a licensed funeral home normally obtains the death certificate and a removal or burial-transit permit before departure. For destinations outside the US, the destination consulate's requirements (embalming, sealed coffin, legalisation) apply. Confirm with the Office of Vital Records (St Thomas or St Croix).
authority: US CDC and CBP (entry); Virgin Islands Department of Health, Office of Vital Records and Statistics (exit)
documents: Death certificate stating the cause of death (English or with a translation), unless the remains are embalmed
Embalming certificate where the body is embalmed
Consular Report of Death Abroad or Consular Mortuary Certificate from the US embassy if the deceased was a US citizen
Removal or export permit from the country of departure
Passport of the deceased and air waybill or flight manifest
Name and contact of the receiving licensed funeral home in US Virgin Islands

at_a_glance.consular: US consular mortuary certificate if needed
at_a_glance.permit: CDC permit only for infectious diseases
at_a_glance.arrival: CBP clearance; licensed funeral home receives

name: Vietnam
summary: A body may enter Vietnam only with a permit from the Vietnamese embassy or consulate in the country of death, which needs prior written consent from the People's Committee (or cemetery) where the body will be buried. The body must travel in a three-layer coffin with a hermetically sealed zinc inner layer, and deaths from transmissible diseases cannot be brought in.
coffin: Vietnamese law (Ministry of Health Circular 21/2021) requires a three-layer coffin for cross-border transport: an inner layer of zinc or other non-leaking load-bearing material, lined with absorbent and hermetically sealed; a wooden middle layer; and a plywood outer layer. Vietnamese embassy guidance (Ottawa, New Delhi) describes a zinc-covered coffin lined with PVC sheets and absorbent material, placed in an outer wooden case sealed by security and health authorities in the country of departure.
embalming: Not explicitly required by the embassy pages consulted. Vietnamese hygiene rules limit holding a body to 48 hours without refrigeration and 7 days refrigerated at 4 C or below, so embalming is in practice expected for air transport.
consular: The Vietnamese embassy or consulate in the country of death issues the entry permit (Circular 01/2011: within 1 working day of a complete file; embassies in Ottawa and New Delhi announce 5 to 7 business days). The permit also cancels the deceased's Vietnamese passport and is notified to border customs and immigration. Group A infectious disease deaths (e.g. Ebola, cholera, SARS, plague) are refused.
arrival: Border customs and health quarantine at the arrival airport check the permit and documents before release to the family or funeral service. Remains must comply with Vietnamese customs and quarantine law.
private_aviation: The embassy permit application names the arrival airport, carrier, flight number and arrival time, so a private flight must be scheduled before the permit is requested. Use an international airport with customs and health quarantine.
export: To take a body out of Vietnam, the funeral director obtains an international medical quarantine certificate (in Hanoi from the International Centre for Disease Control) and permission from the Quarantine and Customs and Immigration Office; a certificate of preservation, the death certificate and passport are also needed. Local authorities require a diplomatic note from the deceased's embassy confirming the family's wishes. Hospitals normally embalm. Local formalities take about one week (gov.uk); the death certificate takes about a week.
authority: Vietnamese embassy or consulate (Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Consular Department); local People's Committee; border health quarantine
documents: Vietnamese embassy permit application form (with landing airport, carrier, flight number and arrival time)
Written consent of the local People's Committee in Vietnam where the body will be buried, obtained by a relative in Vietnam
Death certificate (certified copy)
Applicant's passport or ID and proof of relationship
Deceased's passport and proof of Vietnamese origin where relevant
Certificate of no infectious or contagious disease and local quarantine / transit permit
Funeral director certificate that only the body is in the casket

at_a_glance.embalming: Expected; time limits on holding bodies
at_a_glance.coffin: Three layers, sealed zinc inner coffin
at_a_glance.arrival: Customs and health quarantine at airport

steps.what: A relative in Vietnam requests written consent from the local People's Committee where the body will be buried.
Obtain the death certificate, no-contagious-disease certificate, transit permit and embalming in the country of death.
Prepare the three-layer coffin with sealed zinc inner layer; have the outer case sealed as required.
Apply to the Vietnamese embassy or consulate with the flight details; the permit is issued in 1 to 7 working days depending on the post.
Customs and health quarantine clear the coffin; the family or funeral service collects it for burial.

name: Mayotte (France)
summary: Mayotte is an overseas department of France and follows French rules: from abroad, the French embassy or consulate in the country of death authorises the transport; from mainland France, the prefect of the department where the coffin is closed authorises it. An airtight (metal-lined) coffin is mandatory by air.
coffin: Airtight coffin with a metal box (in practice soldered zinc inside a wooden coffin) is mandatory for air transport under French rules. A hermetic coffin complicates later cremation.
embalming: French rules do not impose embalming for an incoming body; the departure country and airline usually require it for long journeys.
consular: From abroad, entry into France (including overseas departments) and transport to the place of burial or cremation require authorisation from the French embassy or consulate. France is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement; whether a Strasbourg laissez-passer alone suffices for this department is not stated, confirm with the consulate. Families bear all costs.
arrival: The receiving funeral director takes the coffin at the airport. French law (CGCT art. R2213-33) sets burial or cremation no later than the 14th calendar day after the body enters the territory of the overseas department when it comes from abroad; the prefect may grant exceptions. Most of the population is Muslim and families usually seek a rapid burial; prepare paperwork before the flight.
private_aviation: Same documents as airline cargo; the coffin must be airtight for any air transport. Plan arrival at Dzaoudzi-Pamandzi international airport, with customs (douane) and border police, and have the receiving funeral director meet the aircraft. The runway at Dzaoudzi-Pamandzi is short, which limits some long-range jets; check aircraft performance with the operator.
export: The funeral company handles formalities. To mainland France or abroad, the prefect of the department where the coffin is closed authorises the transport; air transport requires an airtight coffin. Ashes need authorisation from the prefect of the place of cremation or of the applicant's residence. The destination country's consular rules also apply.
authority: French embassy or consulate abroad (entry from abroad); Prefect of Mayotte (exit) and prefect where the coffin is closed
documents: Local death certificate (transcription into French civil status by the consulate recommended)
Medical certificate of cause of death or non-contagion certificate
Embalming or conservation certificate where required by the departure country
Transport authorisation from the French embassy or consulate (from abroad) or from the prefect where the coffin is closed (from mainland France or another DOM)
Coffin closure/sealing certificate
Details of the receiving funeral director and cemetery or crematorium

Obtain death certificate, medical certificate and embalming as required
Coffin sealed in airtight zinc-lined coffin; consular or prefect authorisation issued

Local funeral director collects; burial or cremation within 14 days of entry

name: South Africa
summary: A coffin can enter South Africa only with an import permit issued in advance by the National Department of Health (Director-General of Health); no permit is issued at the point of entry. The body must be embalmed (unless religion forbids it) and sealed in an airtight container inside a sturdy non-transparent coffin.
coffin: For non-infectious remains, the body is sealed in an airtight container and placed in a sturdy, non-transparent coffin. Infectious remains must also be placed in a polythene bag, and their sealed container may not be opened without approval of the medical officer (Regulation R363, reg. 12).
embalming: Embalming is required and certified. If embalming cannot be done for religious reasons, a statement from the relevant authority describing the alternative preservation method must be supplied. Bodies of persons who died of smallpox, anthrax or viral haemorrhagic fever must not be embalmed.
consular: A South African embassy or the funeral undertaker can submit the permit application; the Consulate General in New York, for example, sends a request letter with the deceased's particulars to Pretoria. Documents not in English need a certified translation. South Africa is not a party to the Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: Port Health (Border Management Authority) detains and inspects human remains on arrival and grants clearance only once permit conditions are met. Remains arriving without a permit can be held in a mortuary at the importer's cost and, if no permit follows within 30 days, buried by order of the Director-General. A certified local undertaker receives the coffin.
private_aviation: The permit application must name the point of entry and the type of transport, so a private flight must land at the declared port of entry with Port Health (Border Management Authority) presence. The regulations require an airtight container in a sealed coffin on public transport and an approved coffin or container otherwise; confirm acceptable containers with the Department of Health.
export: Leaving South Africa also requires an export permit from the National Department of Health (applied for by email; about 2 working days once complete). The file includes a cover letter naming the exit point and transport, death certificate with cause of death, ID or passport (or a police affidavit), an embalming certificate stamped by the undertaker and embalmer with the address of the embalming premises, a family request letter, a non-infectious disease certificate, the Notice of Death form (BI-1663), the Burial Order from the Department of Home Affairs and the undertaker's Certificate of Competence.
authority: National Department of Health (Director-General of Health); Port Health, Border Management Authority
documents: Import permit from the National Department of Health, applied for by email to humanremainspermits@health.gov.za (valid 30 days)
Cover letter from the embassy or funeral undertaker naming the deceased, place of burial, date, place and cause of death, the South African point of entry and the type of transport
Death certificate clearly stating the cause of death (certified English translation if needed)
ID document or passport of the deceased
Embalming certificate (or statement of the alternative preservation method if embalming is refused for religious reasons)
Letter from a family member requesting the import, with their ID or passport and contact details
Non-infectious (or infectious) disease certificate signed by a registered medical practitioner or forensic pathologist
Certificate of Competence of the South African funeral undertaker who will receive the remains

name: Zambia
summary: Bringing remains into Zambia needs prior written consent from the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Lusaka, requested through the Zambian embassy. The body must be in a hermetically sealed casket inside a wooden outer box, attested by the local health authority.
coffin: Hermetically sealed casket inside a wooden outer box, attested by a notarised statement from the local health authority of the country of death.
embalming: The Zambian embassy checklist (Washington) does not list embalming. Airlines and departure countries usually require it; confirm with the Zambian embassy.
consular: Contact the Zambian embassy's consular section and send a scanned application package; prior written consent comes from the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Lusaka. No fee or processing time is published. Zambia is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: The application must name the Zambian residents who will take charge of the remains. Arrival clearance details are not published; originals should travel with the coffin for customs and health checks.
private_aviation: No published rule specific to private or charter flights was found. Human remains travel with the same documents as on an airline (originals with the coffin), and the aircraft should land at an international airport with customs, immigration and port-health officers on duty; usual landing and overflight permissions for foreign-registered aircraft apply. The zinc-lined coffin (about 2.2 m, often 100 kg or more) must fit the cargo door or a cabin configured for it. Main international airports include Lusaka (Kenneth Kaunda) and Ndola.
export: The UK FCDO guide covers death registration (Registrar General, Lusaka, or local Boma offices; certificates in English, collectable within 48 hours), body identification and release from the morgue by the next of kin or a nominee. It does not detail export permits, embalming or coffin rules or timelines; the funeral director handles them. Post-mortems and police cases can delay release.
authority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Lusaka (Permanent Secretary), via Zambian embassies
documents: Application with the deceased's name and details, reason for the request and tentative transport schedule
Names and addresses of the Zambian residents responsible for the remains in Zambia
Notarised statement from the local health authority that there is no danger of infection
Notarised statement from the local health authority that the body is in a hermetically sealed casket and wooden outer box
Locally issued burial and/or transit permit
Certified copy of the death certificate

at_a_glance.coffin: Hermetically sealed casket in wooden box
at_a_glance.permit: Prior written consent from Foreign Ministry
